Guide / November 2026

Do contractors need a website, or is word of mouth enough?

Most contractors need a website, even busy ones who live on word of mouth. Referred customers still look you up before they call, and a simple site with your services, area, photos, reviews and a phone number is the only place online you fully own. A few trades can get by without one for now, and we show you how to tell which side you are on.

Do contractors need a website?

Yes, for most contractors in 2026, but not for the reason website sellers usually give. A website will not magically fill your diary. What it does is make every other way you get work, from referrals to Google Maps to a van sign, convert better, because it answers the questions people have before they pick up the phone:

  • Do you do the job I need? A list of services, in plain words.
  • Do you work where I live? Your service area, named town by town.
  • Can I trust you? Real job photos, reviews, licences and insurance.
  • How do I reach you? A phone number you can tap and a short form.

If your Facebook page, Google profile or a directory already answers all four questions well, and you are happy with the work you get, you can wait. If any of them is missing, or you want different work from what you get now, a basic site is one of the cheapest fixes you can buy.

I get all my work from word of mouth. Do I still need one?

This is the most common objection on trade forums, and it is a fair one. Plenty of good contractors are booked months ahead without a website. The catch is what happens between the recommendation and the phone call.

When a neighbour says “use Dave, he did our roof”, the customer usually searches for you before calling. BrightLocal's Local Consumer Review Survey 2026 found that 97% of consumers read reviews for local businesses, and that after reading positive reviews, 54% go on to check the business's website. That was 32% when they last asked in 2019. The same survey found 66% of people do more research after a good review rather than booking straight away.

So a referral is a warm lead, not a closed job. If the search turns up nothing, an old Facebook post or a competitor with a smart site and fifty reviews, some of those referrals quietly go elsewhere and you never know they existed. A website protects the word of mouth you have already earned.

It also gives you choice. Word of mouth brings you more of whatever you did last. If you want fewer small repairs and more full renovations, a site with photos and a page for that service is how you start attracting that work on purpose.

When can a contractor get by without a website?

We would rather be honest than sell you something you do not need. These are the situations where a website is genuinely low priority:

  • You only work for two or three builders or companies who send you all the work and never shop around.
  • You are fully booked for a year or more, are not planning to hire, and do not want different work.
  • You are winding down and plan to retire or sell within a year or two.
  • You are just starting out on a tight budget. Set up a free Google Business Profile first, collect reviews from your first jobs, then build a site once you have photos to show.

Even then, keep a strong Google Business Profile. Our Google Business Profile checklist covers every setting that matters. And watch for the signs that it is time: builders you rely on slow down, a quiet season arrives, or you want to raise your prices and need to look like the premium option.

Is a Facebook page or Google Business Profile enough?

They are worth having, and for many trades a Google Business Profile brings more calls than the website does. But each one does a different job, and none of them belongs to you.

Google Business ProfileFacebook or Instagram pageDirectory listingYour own website
Cost to set upFreeFreeFree to paidPaid
Shows in Google MapsYesNoNoHelps your profile rank
Ranks for “service + town” searchesIn the map resultsRarelySometimes, next to rivalsYes, with a page per service
You control the layout and wordingPartlyPartlyBarelyFully
Competitors shown beside youOftenOftenAlwaysNever
Can be suspended or changed by someone elseYesYesYesNo

That last row matters more than people think. In March 2024 Google switched off the free websites it used to offer inside Business Profiles, and Search Engine Land reported that visitors were only redirected to the profile until June 10, 2024. Contractors who relied on those sites lost them on Google's timetable. Profiles also get suspended, sometimes by mistake. Our guide on a suspended Google Business Profile explains how often that catches out trades.

The best setup is all of them working together: the profile and social pages bring people in, and the website is where they land to decide.

Is a website worth the money? A sum to decide

Work it out with your own numbers rather than anyone's sales pitch. You need three figures:

  1. Your average profit per job. Not the job price, the money left after materials, labour and overheads.
  2. The total cost of the site over three years. The build plus hosting, domain and any monthly fee.
  3. How many extra jobs it needs to win to pay for itself: cost divided by profit per job.

Here is an example with round numbers. They show the method and are not a price guide.

ItemExample
Average job price$3,000
Profit on that job at 20%$600
Website, hosting and domain over three years$3,000
Extra jobs needed over three years to break even$3,000 ÷ $600 = 5
Extra jobs needed per yearFewer than 2

If a website helps you win two extra jobs a year, from referrals who checked you out, from Google searches, or from customers who chose you over a cheaper quote because you looked more established, it has paid for itself. For bigger jobs the sum gets even easier. To see what sites really cost where you work, read our guides for the USA, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

What does a basic contractor website need?

You do not need a huge site to start. A small one done properly beats a big one done badly. The minimum we would accept:

  • A clear headline that says what you do and where: “Roof repairs and restorations in Leeds and nearby towns”.
  • A tap to call button at the top on phones, plus a short quote form.
  • One section or page per main service, written the way customers search for it.
  • Your service area, listing the towns or suburbs you cover.
  • Real job photos, ideally before and after, not stock images.
  • Reviews, with a link to your Google reviews.
  • Licences, registrations and insurance, shown plainly.
  • Fast loading on a phone, because that is where most of your visitors will be.

Our full guide to what a trade website needs goes through each page in detail, with the mistakes that cost contractors jobs.

What a website will not do on its own

Be wary of anyone who promises a flood of leads from a new site alone. A website is a shop window. People still have to walk past it. On its own, a brand new site with no reviews and no Google profile behind it will get very few visitors for months.

What makes it work:

  • A complete Google Business Profile that links to the site.
  • A steady trickle of fresh reviews. See how to get Google reviews for the texts to send.
  • Local SEO basics, such as service pages and consistent business details. Our local SEO guide for trades covers them.
  • Putting your website address everywhere: your van, quotes, invoices, email signature and business cards.

Done together, these turn the site from a brochure into something that brings in work.

What does a contractor website have to show by law?

This depends on where you work, so treat this as a starting point. In California, the Contractors State License Board advertising guidelines say licensed contractors must include their licence number in advertising, and that covers websites. Many other states, provinces and countries have similar rules for licence or registration numbers. In the UK, limited companies generally have to show their registered name, company number and registered office address on their website. Check with your licensing body or trade association what yours needs, and put it in the footer so it appears on every page.

This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

How to get started this week

The hardest part is usually gathering the material, not building the site. Start collecting it now:

  1. Pick your three main services and the work you want more of.
  2. List the towns or suburbs you are happy to drive to.
  3. Go through your phone and save your 20 best job photos into one folder.
  4. Ask five happy past customers for a review. Copy this text:

“Hi Maria, it was great working on your kitchen last spring. I am putting together a new website and it would really help if you could leave a quick Google review about the job. Here is the link. Thanks again, Tom.”

And if you want to use a photo of a past job at someone's home, ask first:

“Hi Maria, would you mind if I used a couple of photos of your finished kitchen on my website? No address or names, just the work. Totally fine if not.”

Once you have the services, the area, the photos and a few reviews, any decent web designer can turn them into a site quickly, and you will get a much better result than starting from a blank page.

Do this now

Your checklist.

  1. 01Search your own business name on a phone and see what a referred customer finds
  2. 02Set up or complete your free Google Business Profile
  3. 03Do the break even sum with your own profit per job
  4. 04Pick your three main services and the work you want more of
  5. 05List the towns or suburbs you cover
  6. 06Save your 20 best job photos into one folder
  7. 07Ask five past customers for a Google review
  8. 08Check what licence or company details your website must show
Quick answers

Common questions.

Can a contractor get work without a website?

Yes. Many get by on word of mouth, builders and a Google Business Profile. But referred customers often search for you before calling, and without a site some of them choose someone who looks more established.

Is a Facebook page enough for a contractor?

It helps, but it rarely ranks for searches like “electrician near me”, it shows competitors beside you, and you do not control it. Use it alongside a website, not instead of one.

Do I need a website to be on Google Maps?

No. A Google Business Profile does not need a website. Linking one to your profile does give customers more reasons to trust you and helps your profile make sense to Google.

Does Google still give businesses a free website?

No. Google switched off the websites built inside Business Profiles in 2024, and their links stopped redirecting to the profile in June 2024.

How many pages does a contractor website need?

A small site with a home page, a section or page for each main service, a service area page, photos, reviews and a contact page is enough to start. Add pages as you add services.

Will a website get me more leads on its own?

Rarely. A website converts the people who find you. Pair it with a complete Google Business Profile, fresh reviews and basic local SEO to bring visitors in.
